subject: treeSloth
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: three-toed sloth hanging from a branch.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm scoping out a sizable module, planning for roughly 600-900 lines since I won't be able to test it directly, so I need to be careful with the API usage. I'm weighing distinctive visual styles for the sloth design—something like Andean textile patchwork or Peruvian arpillera—to make it stand out.

I'll commit to a felt-and-embroidery folk-art plush look: flat felt colors with stitched seams, blanket-stitch edges on patches, and button eyes with a signature dark eye-mask patch. Now I'm thinking through the composition—a three-toed sloth hanging upside-down from a horizontal branch, sketching out rough body and arm proportions to ground the scene.

For the orientation, I'm deciding to run the branch along the Z axis with the sloth's body parallel to it, head pointed toward +Z so it faces the viewer since the model faces +Z. This keeps the pose natural—sloth belly-up gripping the branch with all four limbs—while letting the head turn forward to engage the camera.

Now I'm figuring out the vertical layout: branch center around y=0.62 with a thin 0.04 radius, and the sloth's body hanging below it with the chest around 0.12 radius and arms roughly 0.35 long reaching up to hook claws over the branch, making sure the lowest point of the model still touches y=0.

Checking lowest point of body and head against the floor, nothing quite reaches y=0 yet, so I need to shift the whole figure down until its lowest point actually touches the ground.

Keeping the sloth's scale realistic, around 0.6-0.7m tall when hanging, I'm figuring out the body's vertical center and how the branch position relates to it, while considering adding dangling details like claws hooking over the branch and hind legs reaching up for a more natural hanging pose.

I'm working through the exact coordinates: body center around y=0.16 with radius 0.15 so the bottom barely touches the floor, the head positioned slightly forward and higher to face outward, and making sure the shaggy fur card details on the back don't dip below the ground plane -- I may need to shrink or filter out any cards that would poke through.

Now I'm positioning the branch and working out the shoulder-to-branch geometry, figuring the arm lengths and bend angles needed for the hands to reach the branch, with elbows bending outward and back to span the distance.

For the hands and feet, I'm planning three curved claws each that hook over the top of the branch while the paw itself rests against its side, treating the branch as a cylinder along the Z axis.

Working out the claw geometry now, curving each claw from the palm up and over the branch top to grip the far side, with tapering radius and tight z-spacing between claws...

Still working out claw arc geometry...

Then I need to add a felt mitten blob between wrist and claws, with three claws per limb spaced at small z offsets relative to each hand joint. I'm also sketching out the overall body proportions — rump to chest along z, head extending further, totaling roughly 0.6 length for the sloth.

The branch itself should extend well beyond the body with small stubs, styled as brown felt with stitched ring bands for grain and a few green leaf appliqués with stitched veins for texture. For the body, I'm planning a catmull spline sweep along the spine from hips to chest with varying radius, letting it sag naturally as a hanging form.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton: a root hips joint, then a spine chain built with catmull points running from hips through to the upper torso, parented correctly so the chain starts cleanly at the hips without redundant joints.

For the neck I'm defining a short chain from the chest to the head base using three catmull points producing two named joints, parented to the last spine joint. Then I'm adding a separate head joint parented to the neck tip, positioned near z≈0.3-0.38 and y≈0.27-0.28, with its own orientation.

Now I'm shaping the head as an ellipsoid roughly 0.095 wide centered around (0, 0.285, 0.375), then building a small muzzle structure: an upper snout sphere scaled down for the sloth's stubby face, a dark felt nose oval at the tip, and a tiny lower jaw sphere hinged below it on a jaw bone, with a smile line meant to curve upward at the corners like a stitched decal.

I'm planning the facial texture as a decal on the skull: a cream face patch with dark eye-stripe "mask" markings extending toward the cheeks, edged with stitch dashes, and button eyes made from a small cylinder with a textured plane showing two stitched cross-thread holes, oriented outward on the head.

Next I'm sketching the body felt paint — a warm oatmeal-brown fur base with an algae-sage tint and cream/dark accents, meant to mimic felt fibers with stitched appliqué seams.

I'm thinking of making the piece a colour-blocked folk toy: oatmeal felt body with sage and terracotta patches, cream stitching, plus a decorative embroidered leaf-and-flower decal on the back and a couple of flank patches for visual interest.

For fur texture, I'm planning jagged felt tuft cards scattered across the body — around 250 cards at 4 triangles each — drawn in grey-white gradient so they can be tinted by a fur paint color at the root.

Now I'm thinking through a felt-style helper function that mixes a base color with fine fiber noise for a fabric-like surface variation.

I'm also planning dashed seam stitching along the belly and side lines using cream thread, and estimating texel density for the 1024px paint sheet relative to the model's painted surface area.

Given the sloth hangs upside-down, I realize the belly faces the branch at the "top" (deg near 0), so the paler cream patch belongs there, while the back is sage-brown with the embroidered decal on the "bottom" side.

Writing body shape code...

I'm adding a small cream tail stub at the rump, then sweeping the neck with tapering radii and overlapping the head sphere, before starting on limb placement with shoulder joints positioned at the body's sides.

Working out the arm geometry now, placing the shoulder joint just inside the body surface and computing the hand and wrist target positions for the claw arc.

The shoulder-to-wrist distance comes out to about 0.185, well under the two-segment reach of 0.34, so the elbow needs a pronounced bend outward and slightly back to look natural rather than straight.

I'm computing the elbow's outward offset using the Pythagorean relation between arm segment length and midpoint distance, landing around x≈0.21 for a splayed elbow, which matches how sloths actually hold their arms — though that's a bit wide relative to the body's half-width of 0.14, so trimming segments to 0.15/0.16 brings the offset down to about 0.19, which reads better while keeping arms proportionally longer than the legs. Now I'm setting up the hind leg hip joint and its target wrist position with a different z-depth than the arms.

I'm checking that the branch clears above the head with enough gap, and adjusting the neck position to angle slightly toward it. Then I'm setting up the joint hierarchy for the limbs, with arms chaining off the upper spine and legs off the base, each named shoulder/elbow/wrist or hip/knee/ankle for the three-point chain.

Now I'm defining the claw digits: three claws per limb across four limbs, each with two joints, parented to the wrist or ankle, using a short arc path with names that set the resample count to two segments.

I'm sweeping the claw chain with tapering radii and flat-to-point caps, keeping total skeleton joints around 45—well under the 160 budget—with digits properly parented to each limb's tip joint.

For the arms, I'm sweeping a smooth tube with shrinking radius for the sloth's shaggy limbs, then scattering fur-tuft cards across the surface. I'm weighing how many distinct textured parts that generates, since each differently-colored card batch likely counts as a separate mesh part.

For the hand, I'm capsule-sweeping a dark brown felt paw from wrist to claw base, adding small knuckle spheres, and anchoring it rigidly off the wrist joint. Now I'm starting to think through how to construct the head region for the face.

For the head, I'm placing the skull as a scaled sphere at a fixed center point, giving it round proportions with a short snout, then adding a lighter cream face mask decal with stitched-border eye patches slanting outward to give that classic bandit-eyed sloth look, with the button eyes sitting on top of the patches.

Now I'm working out the decal geometry and SVG path for the cream face shape itself, plus a stitched smile below the muzzle and pink felt blush circles on the cheeks.

For the eye mask, I'm shaping dark brown rotated ellipses as the sloth's signature stripe patches, extending outward and downward from each eye with stitched edges to mimic felt applique.

Converting the eye pixel positions into normalized sphere coordinates, I'm working out where each eye should sit relative to the head's center and radius so they land symmetrically on the curved surface.

Instead of hand-computing the surface math, I'll use a ray-casting approach: shoot a ray from the front toward the skull surface to get the hit point and normal, then stick a small button cylinder there aligned to that normal, with a flat circular face texture layered just above it.

I'm settling the exact embed depth so the texture sits just above the surface, then designing the button texture itself: a dark brown disc with a lighter ring, four stitch holes with a cream thread cross, and a small specular highlight — essentially making a glossy black-bead eye look using this button motif.

Now I'm placing the nose and snout geometry, protruding a short blunt muzzle forward from the face at the right coordinates, then planning the smile as a stitched thread curve swept along the snout's surface using control points to get that signature sloth grin.

I'm reconsidering whether the smile should instead be a decal projected onto both the skull and snout surfaces together, adjusting projection segments for smoothness, and figuring out how the lower jaw piece fits beneath the snout so the mouth line sits naturally at that junction.

Working out the smile curve coordinates on the snout decal, placing the mouth line around pixel y=122 with corners sweeping upward like a sloth's grin, and checking the curve width fits within the snout's projected surface bounds.

I'm also figuring out how the jaw sits relative to the smile line — making sure the jaw ellipsoid stays recessed behind the snout surface so the stitched smile reads clearly on top, with the jaw visible as a separate shape just below where the decal ends.

I'll just use a decal instead of a separate sweep thread for the smile. For the nose, I'm placing a dark felt ellipse by ray-casting onto the snout tip. Then I'm adding tiny hidden ear nubs tucked at the sides of the head, plus fur tuft cards scattered across the skull and forehead for texture.

Now I'm filtering which hits get tufts, excluding the face region to avoid covering the eyes and mouth. Skipping stitched eyebrows. For the back decal, I'm placing it on the body sweep near the bottom-back, orienting it downward with an appropriate up-vector and sizing it to fit the texture's aspect ratio.

But then I realize a key issue: the sloth hangs with its back facing down, so the viewer from above or front barely sees any back decal. I should instead reposition the more elaborate embroidery (stem, leaves, flowers, diamond border) onto the visible flanks and lower sides, using angled dir vectors like [s, -0.3, 0] so they're actually seen, while keeping a smaller rosette/mandala motif as secondary flank decoration.

I'm also considering the belly surface visible from above when hanging, giving it a cream felt treatment with dotted stitch rows, versus the oatmeal sides/back trimmed with a zigzag blanket-stitch border -- splitting the body paint logic by angular region.

Working out the dorsal clock-angle math...

Still defining the felt tone helper...

For the arms, I'm thinking of giving the forearm a darker brown shade than the upper arm using a threshold on the sweep parameter, and now I'm sketching a jagged felt tuft card as a tapering grey shape with a thin stitched centerline for texture.

I'm figuring out that the drawing's bottom edge should sit on the frame root, meaning the pointed tip of the tuft needs to be oriented toward the top of the SVG.

Still writing shape code...

I'm also planning variety: a jagged double-tip tuft variant, and a small green moss-colored card for algae patches on the sloth's back, sparingly scattered. Then I'm figuring out how card tinting works by reading the coat paint color at the card's root, and starting to think through the overall card count budget.

Now I'm working out fur flow direction — since the sloth hangs upside-down, fur should drip toward gravity, so I'm defining a flow vector pointing down and slightly back, with a fallback direction for surfaces where that flow becomes degenerate (like flat top-facing belly normals), switching to a backward flow in those cases.

Mirror symmetry for the card faces doesn't matter here since they're symmetric either way. For scattering cards on the branch and body surfaces, I'm using the scatter function with distance and filter constraints, and defining the branch's curved sweep path with slight waviness along its length, keeping the deviation small so it still reads as a mostly straight branch.

I'll make the branch a simple straight rod with a nearly constant radius around 0.036, faceted rather than smooth, checking that it clears the claw arcs with enough gap. Since it's a static, unrigged part of the model, it doesn't need bone weighting like the other components.

Thinking about the skeleton structure, I decide to keep the hips as the first spine joint, with a root joint at [0,0.2,0] near the origin, and treat the branch as attached to that root since it stays static relative to the body.

For the branch texture, I'm planning a felt-wrapped look with a brown diagonal spiral stitch pattern, computing the stitch lines procedurally and setting the branch length to 1.35.

Still writing spiral stitch math...

I also want to add palmate leaf appliqués near both ends of the branch—a few simple green felt leaves tilted and extruded, with a center vein stitched in thread. I'm sketching the leaf outline shape now to define its curved palmate form.

Computing a proper perpendicular y-vector for the leaf frame, then sketching vein patterns using coordinate masks for the center line and chevron side veins, with lighter thread coloring. I'm also considering adding a small stitched hibiscus flower with petals arranged in a ring near the branch.

Actually, flower geometry is getting overly complex for the payoff here—I'll drop the standalone flower and instead work small stitched flowers into the embroidery decals, keeping it simpler while still adding floral detail. For texture variety, I'll add green felt moss/algae tufts on the back and shoulders.

For the tail, I'm working out a small joint chain sprouting from the rump, using a surface raycast to find the attachment point and sprouting two tapered segments outward and down to form a short tail stub.

Then I'm setting up a jaw joint hinged under the head, aimed slightly forward to establish the jaw hinge's local orientation, followed by the head joint itself parented to the top of the neck chain.

For the neck, I'm defining a two-joint chain ("neck1", "neck2") parented at the base of the neck, with the head joint positioned at the top end pointing slightly upward and forward. Then I'm placing the skull part rigidly bound to the head bone at its computed center point, figuring out whether the scale option should accept a number or a vector.

Since I'm unsure if `part()` accepts vector scale directly, I'll instead scale the sphere geometry itself before creating the part, since BufferGeometry.scale properly transforms normals via the normal matrix. I'll write an ellipsoid helper that builds pre-scaled geometry, and consider using the flat-shading option for a faceted low-poly look.

For the plush, rounded aesthetic I want, I decide smooth shading with fewer segments works better than flat faces. I'm also checking that surface-sticking and ray-hit detection on parts still work correctly when the underlying geometry has been scaled -- confirming they operate on the built triangles, which should be fine.

Writing SVG face decal...

I'm converting the patch center coordinates into 3D head-space positions, checking the eye spacing fits within the head width, and sizing the patch radius relative to the eye button radius.

Still planning facial details... adjusting patch dimensions, adding brow tufts, cheek blush circles, and a cream muzzle patch with a dashed border and stitched smile line.

Checking the projection math for how the decal wraps onto the curved snout, since positions far from center get distorted by the orthographic mapping along the z-axis.

I'll bump segment resolution to 28 for smoother decal coverage and set a small lift so it doesn't clip into the buttons protruding above. For the lower jaw, I'm keeping it a simple cream felt ellipsoid without teeth or tongue detail, then moving on to designing the embroidered flank decal with a stem, leaves, and a flower motif in the SVG.

Writing SVG decal code...

Now thinking about a second flank decal: a rosette design with concentric ring stitching and eight petals in mustard and teal, deciding whether to place it on the hips or upper arms versus the flora motif on the flanks.

I should set the decal's up vector to world +Y so flowers appear stem-up naturally, and then work out mirroring: checking which world axis corresponds to the viewer's right when looking at the left flank from +X, to make sure mirrored decals read correctly on both sides.

Since the floral motif is roughly symmetric anyway, I can skip worrying about mirror orientation. I'll also skip adding a belly decal for now, and instead focus on making sure fur cards scattered on the body don't poke through the flank decal regions by filtering out hits that land within the decal's placement area.

Defining the exclusion zone...

Then I'll move on to scattering fur tufts on each arm as flat felt-strip cards, about fourteen per arm.

For the body sweep, I'm using the chain as the source for the decal and setting up the body profile along the spine, with the body's radius tapering from the hips through the torso and a rounded cap at the rump, keeping the join to the neck simple.

Still shaping arm proportions, with thicker upper arms tapering to narrower forearms, plus a stitched cuff band near the wrist for texture. Now I'm sketching out the paw shape as a rounded sphere form.

Modeling the paw as a capsule from wrist to claw base, using dark felt coloring, with small knuckle spheres at each claw's root. I'm spreading three claw bases across the z-axis so they fan out slightly, then checking that the paw's radius is wide enough to fully cover that spread plus the claw thickness.

Switching the paw shape to an ellipsoid instead of a capsule for a more natural rounded form, sized around 0.028 by 0.03 by 0.042 and positioned at the midpoint between wrist and claw start, attached to the wrist bone. For the claws themselves, I'm using long 105° arcs at radius 0.05 to get realistic sloth-like claw length, tapering from a 0.011 base radius, colored in cream felt tubing with a darker tip accent.

Setting up chain generation for each claw as a two-joint arc bound to the wrist, with naming conventions that satisfy identifier rules while staying unique across all twelve claw chains.

Checking the other claw's rotation direction (s=-1): starting near 200° and sweeping clockwise through 180° and 135° down to about 95°, confirming both claws converge near the top around 85-95° and overlap there.

Since both left and right claws converge to the same region at top, I need to stagger them in z so they don't collide — adjusting hand z-offsets so left claws sit around 0.195-0.235 and right claws around 0.165-0.205, checking the small overlap zone against the tapered claw tip radius.

For the hind legs I'll mirror the same gripping pose, placing hips at a symmetric offset and wrists near the branch, keeping three toes/claws consistent with the front limbs.

I'm defining a buildLimb helper that constructs each limb's chain of named joints (shoulder/elbow/wrist for arms, hip/knee/ankle for legs), feeding the point arrays into a skinning chain so corners round smoothly into the body mesh.

For fur and surface detail, I'm scattering fur cards along the arm sweep with density and minimum distance constraints, filtering out cards facing downward so they don't clump underneath. I'm also sizing the neck sweep radius for a tapered coat, and planning shaggy fringe tufts along the top of the head for that sloth-like hooded look.

I'm filtering skull cards to exclude the front face region while keeping them along the top, sides, and back, with the forehead fringe hanging down to drape over the brow without covering the eyes, using a steep lean angle so they fall naturally.

Since the head sits upright while the body hangs, fur flows downward from the top of the head and along the body, with belly fur flowing backward parallel to the spine axis. Now I'm setting up the felt color palette, starting with the oat tone for the coat paint.

Writing more palette hex values...

I'm also drafting the overall style note describing this as a felt-appliqué folk-art plush with needle-felted wool, stitched seams, button eyes, and embroidered motifs hanging from a thread-wrapped branch, then starting a helper function for tone variations.

Writing the fiber noise function...

Still working through the body color zones...

Still writing bark paint logic...

Adjusting the arc and claw radii so the inner surface stays tangent, settling on roughly 0.052 with tapered claws around 0.042. Then I'm working out where the hand/wrist point sits relative to the shoulder joint to check the reach distance for the limb geometry.

Now I'm computing elbow offsets using the leg length triangle with the hip, wrist target, and bend hint vector — getting an outward splay around 0.2 for the arm, and checking the hip-to-target distances for the legs to confirm the segment lengths work out geometrically before moving on to the head joint placement.

I'm also tallying up the total part count: body, neck, head pieces, arm sweeps with paws, claws, and knuckle spheres, card meshes, decals, branch with leaves and stems, and tail — landing around 80, which is well short of the 180-340 target, so I need to add more detail like stitching sweeps and maybe small felt accessories to bulk it out.

For the texture set, I'm settling on roughly eight distinct maps: two fur tufts, moss, face, button, flora, rosette, and shoulder patch, plus considering appliqué-style round patches on the shoulders and stitched claw rings as additional detail elements.

As a fun extra, I'm thinking of adding a small hanging felt tag from the branch with embroidered "ZZZ" text, extruded in teal with a textured plane on both faces, positioned low enough to dangle without touching the floor.

Since a plane texture only faces one direction, I need separate front and back planes for the tag's decal to show from both sides. I'm also reconsidering its depth placement since putting it too far forward would place it awkwardly in front of the head from the camera's view.

Instead, I think I'll move the tag to hang behind the sloth near the rump, oriented so its face points sideways rather than forward, so it reads clearly from a side angle without clashing with the head.

For the tag itself, I'm planning a small SVG design with a cute "zzZ" and moon motif rather than trying to fit longer text like "take it slow."

For structure, I'll give the branch parts a root joint so everything attaches cleanly to a single bone reference.

I'm reviewing the builder API surface—joints, chains, sweeps, parts, sticks, decals, cards, surfaces, and extrude—to make sure I'm using each function's parameters correctly as I assemble the sloth.

I'm working out the tail sprout call with two joints, making sure the ray origin sits outside the rump so the hit lands correctly on the surface. I'm also setting the jaw joint role and confirming the tuft cards fallback works, then figuring out how the flow function should use the hit's normal to pick direction.

Writing tuft SVG path...

Still writing shape paths...

Actually for a button-eye look, I'll drop the thread-X holes idea and instead make it a dark bead eye with white highlight ellipses and a dashed cream stitched ring around the edge.

I'm sizing the button eye disc proportionally and making sure textured parts only render front-facing geometry using the correct axis orientation; I'll skip adding a glow effect and move on to writing the module code carefully.

Setting up imports...

Still writing shading helper...

Writing paint logic...

Wait, I need to check the actual stitch width in millimeters — my 2.6° angle threshold translates to roughly 12mm on the circumference, which is too wide for a realistic stitch, so I should narrow that to around 1.1° for a 5mm band. The zigzag amplitude and dash spacing otherwise seem reasonable given the pitch and circumference.

Now I'm adding faint cream stripe rows to the belly region using dash-based masking, plus rounded end caps for the rump using simple t=0 angle checks. For the arm paint function, I'm defining a wavy boundary line using a zigzag offset and measuring distance from it in millimeters to control stitch width.

For wrist cuffs I'm adding a terra-toned band near t=0.9–0.94 with thin thread lines marking its edges. Legs reuse this same paint function with a different length parameter, and branch and leaf surfaces get their own base felt colors with thread veining on the leaves. Now I'm moving on to applying flora decals onto the body sweep surface.

For the head, I'm setting up constants for head position and scale, then defining the skull as an ellipsoid shape using those head-scaled radii. For the eyes, I'm casting rays from the front of the face into the skull/snout surface to find where they intersect, which will position the eye sockets correctly on the head geometry.

Checking the circle front face sizing against the cylinder top, then skipping eyebrow stitch details for now. Setting the skull's paint to reuse the coat color and defining the snout as an ellipsoid shape.

Still positioning head parts...

Scattering moss cards onto body surfaces filtered by normal direction, then adding a few onto arms, and setting up twigs sprouting from branch points with leaves attached near their tips.

Placing leaves at several branch positions front and back, skipping the middle where the sloth sits, and checking that the tallest leaf tip stays around 0.7 in height, keeping the whole model within a reasonable bounding box above the floor. I'm also considering hanging a tag near one of the back branch positions.

Writing thread loop geometry...

Then I'm shaping the tag outline as a small extruded pentagon-like shape with a rounded hole-top, painting it a teal felt color at the string's end.

Positioning twin planes front and back of the tag for the TAG texture, each offset slightly so neither z-fights, oriented so the text reads correctly from its own viewing side without mirroring.

I'm sizing the plane to match the tag outline, mapping the tag's rectangular shape with its notched top corners onto an SVG viewBox and scaling the polygon points accordingly.

I'm defining the tag's SVG with a teal fill, dashed stitch border, dark punch hole, and "zZz" text styled in a bold serif font with a moon shape alongside. For the body geometry, I'm weighing sides count for the sweep profile—leaning toward 12 sides for a smoother, plush felt look rather than a low-poly faceted one.

Now I'm writing the limb builder function that computes root, wrist, and bend points for forelimbs and hindlimbs, mirroring positions by side using the sign multiplier. Writing limb geometry logic...

The provided names take precedence, so the chain gets named armL directly. I'm checking the parent joint positions—spine's third joint sits near z=0.08 close to the shoulder at z=0.1, while the hip joint at z=-0.19 lines up reasonably with the leg's z=-0.24 attachment point.

Working out the joint hierarchy now: root sits near the origin, and the spine chain's joints are labeled hips, spine1, spine2, with "hips" serving as the first joint for the spine role. I'm setting up the sweep call to render each chain with its paint color and sides based on chain length, then placing the paw part at the chain's tip using the forced-non-null tip joint, and looping through claw positions offset along the z-axis around the branch.

Now I'm defining the claw digit chains—computing each claw's starting point from an arc around the branch, building a small finger-like chain with named joints, and sweeping it with a color function that switches from claw color to claw-tip color partway along the tube so the color break aligns cleanly. I also add a small knuckle ellipsoid at the claw's base point, and I'm checking that this base point sits just inside the paw's rounded top so the claw root is naturally hidden by the paw geometry.

Now I'm thinking about adding a stitched thread cuff around the wrist for each limb—using a loop cut across the arm chain near its tip (rather than right at the tip, to avoid landing on the rounded cap), then sweeping a thin thread-colored tube around that loop to simulate stitching.

I want two rings framing a terracotta band (around 0.88 and 0.94 along the arm) to form a decorative cuff, and I'm checking that the loop function will correctly isolate the smallest ring around the arm surface rather than accidentally grabbing loops from the torso. Next I'm planning round appliqué patches at the elbow and knee joints, finding the right surface point there to attach a textured rosette.

Working out placement for shoulder rosettes and body-side flora decals...

Checking that body radius matches the rosette placement looks fine. For decals I'll just rely on nearest-hit behavior if a ray fails. For fur cards, I'm writing a filter that skips cards near the flank by checking the hit normal's x-component and the hit position's y/z bounds, so fur doesn't render over that patch.

I'm scattering about 220 cards over the body surface with a minimum spacing of 0.03, which comfortably fits the available surface area. Card sizes range from 0.045 to 0.07, leaning 58 degrees with a 25-degree bend across two segments, flowing downward near the belly top. I'm also scattering around 14 cards per arm with a wider normal filter and slightly larger minimum spacing, plus some mossy cards on the back, and making sure belly cards pick up the coat tint color from the root region.

I realize using the body paint directly for cards would default to a zero position and always render cream, so I need a separate tint function for cards that checks the surface normal: steep upward-facing normals get the cream tone, everything else samples the coat color, using a threshold around 0.4 to roughly match the 66-degree angle cutoff. The neck and head will just use the coat paint directly since they don't need this special treatment.

Now I'm skipping extra decorative details like a stitched spine or claw polish, and moving on to computing the actual skeleton geometry: defining the spine as a sequence of points running from the lower back up toward the neck, then building the neck path as a short curve branching off the spine's last joint with its own tapering radius, leading into the head position just beyond the neck's end point.

I'm sanity-checking the overall proportions -- body length plus the head extension comes out longer than a real sloth but reads fine for a cartoony plush toy, so I'll leave it as is and move toward finalizing the code.

Now I'm working through the API details: how `at` and `dir` accept vectors, how the card-generation function takes a frame and index to determine direction, and how texture arrays get passed into `cards()` along with a seeded RNG. I'm also starting to define the leaf paint function, which samples UV coordinates to drive the pattern.

For the leaf shape itself, I'm sketching outline points to form a sharp-tipped leaf profile, then extruding it. I'm weighing whether to type the outline as a separate `OutlinePoint[]` variable or just inline the array literal directly in the extrude call to dodge typing issues around the "sharp" marker — inlining it seems safer and simpler.

For veining, I'm defining a paint function that detects whether a surface point falls near the midline or the diagonal side veins, and if so applies a dashed thread color pattern instead of the base tone, giving the leaf a stitched vein texture.

I'm skipping tongue details on the jaw, and considering small stitched eyelash or brow details—thinking of using a draped catmull-rom curve across a few points above each eye to create a thick stitched brow line on the skull surface.

Setting brow color to a dark brown, placing them just above the eye region, then checking for leftover unused TypeScript variables before starting to write the actual code.

Setting up imports...

Writing SVG markup...

Simplifying leaves into grouped ellipses with vein lines, each rotated as a unit for a cleaner structure...

Now positioning the leaf placements along the stem and starting to build out the flower petals in a circular arrangement...

Still writing SVG code...

Now I'm thinking through the decal placement details, figuring out the size and position on the face so it sits correctly on the surface.

The decal quads should project along the ray direction onto the outermost surface hit first, which works since the eye buttons sit 7mm in front of the decal. Now I'm working out ear positions on the skull sides.

I'm setting up a filter to exclude forehead cards that face forward, keeping decoration off the front of the face, then shrinking card sizes and adding variation and spin parameters before moving on to sprout the tail geometry.

I'm raycasting into the body surface to find a hit point near the rump, then sprouting two tail segments outward from that point with a stub length around 7cm, checking that the tip direction and parenting to the heaviest nearby bone (the hips) make sense. Now I'm defining the cream-toned paint function for the tail color.

Next I'm setting up the dark brown paw paint, then thinking through how chain naming interacts with joint naming to avoid conflicts across limbs.
